newsitem.title: UK: Hot lotus may warm friendly bugs - scientists.
newsitem.headline: Hot lotus may warm friendly bugs - scientists.

text.p: An Asian lotus flower that can create its own heat probably creates a cozy, warm space for pollinating insects, Australian researchers said on Wednesday.
Roger Seymour and Paul Schultze-Motel, zoologists at the University of Adelaide, said the sacred lotus had an almost unique ability to produce and regulate heat.
It can regulate its own temperature in much in the same way that birds and mammals do, they wrote in a letter to the science journal Nature.

"In air temperatures varying between 10 and 30 degrees C (50 and 86 degrees F), the flowers remain between 30 and 35 degrees C (86 and 95 degrees F) throughout a two to four day period," they said, saying the flowers seemed to use starch to produce the heat.
Only two other plants, one a philodendron, have been shown to have the same ability. Others flowers produce heat but do not control it in such a precise way.
Scientists think heat could help the flowers to spread their scent more effectively or may protect them from cold.
Seymour and Schultze-Motel said the lotus could be rewarding the insects that pollinate it. Insects cannot generate body heat like animals can but need to be warm to fly.

"The environment in the floral chamber would maintain a high body temperature for the insect and promote not only feeding, digestion and reproductive behaviour, but also suitable body temperatures for flight," the zoologists said.
